1033:
Your trucks reached Kunshan after dark. The Scarlet Guards were sitting by the tracks. Some had fallen asleep against the embankment, and some were gnawing cold steamed buns. You jumped down from the truck and shouted at them to go back to Shanghai.

Someone looked up at you. A man stood up and said, isn't that ⟦0⟧.

What came next happened fast. You remembered someone grabbing the collar of your padded jacket. You remembered the gravel underfoot. You remembered someone shouting stop hitting him, and the one shouting was on the Scarlet Guard side.

You were carried back to Shanghai on January 2. A fractured skull, three broken ribs.

You heard the January 6 rally at People's Square over the radio in a hospital bed. The Urgent Notice of January 9 and the Center's congratulatory telegram of January 11 did not have your name on them. People from Workers' General Headquarters came to see you and brought a silk banner that said Wounded for the Revolution.

The banner hung on the ward wall. In the next bed was a Scarlet Guard, also hurt at Kunshan, with his leg in a cast. The two of you shared the room for a month and never spoke to each other. The day he left the hospital, his wife came to get him, and on her way out she filled the thermos by your bed.
1034:
The January Storm happened anyway. At the rally on January 6, the men reading the denunciations on the rostrum were Pan Guoping and Huang Jinhai. On February 5, one of the deputy directors of the Shanghai People's Commune was a worker, Wang Xiuzhen.

After you left the hospital you went back to WGHQ. By then you ranked seventh or eighth. In August 1967, when they were smashing the Liansi, you were in the rear handling stretchers. That summer the Chairman watched a struggle session on television in Shanghai and asked who the young man on the stage was. It was not you.

Later you were vice chairman of a district revolutionary committee. After 1976 you were investigated for two years, given a verdict of “committed serious errors,” and sent back to the mill to labor. There is a scar on your skull, and in winter it hurts when a hat presses on it.

The view changes. You are Lu Genbao again.

On the morning of the 30th you walked out of Kangping Road. Your armband was gone and your padded jacket was missing a button. You did not go home. A lot of people had gathered near North Station. Someone said to go to Beijing and reason it out with Chairman Mao. You went along.

You walked along the railway. You knew this route. A month and a half ago you had ridden the No. 14 express along this same stretch. Many people got on the vehicles back to Shanghai. You stood at the door for a while. You thought of what your wife had said, and of the leaflet folded in your jacket pocket. The vehicle pulled away. You had not got on. You walked on north with the six or seven thousand who remained.

History On the afternoon of the 31st the Scarlet Guards heading north reached Kunshan, and in the clash some trains on the Shanghai-Nanjing line were held up. On January 3, 1967, Ma Tianshui and others rushed to Kunshan to persuade them to return. In the end six or seven thousand still went to Beijing. This became known as the Kunshan Incident. See Wikipedia, “Kangping Road Incident” and “January Storm” (search summary).

1049:
Back at the Mills

On January 5, Workers' General Headquarters, together with Red Guard and other organizations, nine in all, issued an order welcoming Scarlet Guards back to Shanghai and back to their factories. It said the “misled class brothers” should be met with unity, criticism, unity, and that treating ordinary Scarlet Guards as enemies was utterly wrong. It asked the Municipal Party Committee to guarantee their personal safety and factory leaders to protect them from economic persecution. History See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5.

Once they were back, things varied widely from factory to factory. Some factories welcomed them with gongs and drums. Some made them stand at the gate and write self-criticisms. Many ordinary Scarlet Guards never joined any organization again. Some of their headquarters leaders were locked up, and some were denounced by their own members. The Municipal Party Committee the Scarlet Guards had set out to protect was overthrown at People's Square on January 6.

Li Xun sees Shanghai as an exception. After the Kangping Road Incident, Wang Hongwen firmly pushed to bring conservatives into rebel organizations in large numbers. This broke up the conservatives emotionally and organizationally, and conservative organizations ceased to exist in Shanghai. Most provinces were different. There, conservatives later regrouped with the backing of revolutionary committees and the army units sent to Support the Left, such as the “Million Heroes” in Wuhan and the “Alliance Command” in Guangxi. History See Li Xun, “The Neglected History: On Taking the Study of Cultural Revolution Conservatives Seriously.” This is also why the game's lenient choices have some historical basis.

The conservatives did not simply vanish. In the Shanghai Diesel Liansi of summer 1967 and in the investigations after October 1976, you can see traces of old scores between the two factions. These come up again in later acts. Interpretation
1050:
On January 5, Workers' General Headquarters and eight other organizations jointly issued an order welcoming Scarlet Guards back to Shanghai and back to their factories. It said misled class brothers should be met with unity, criticism, unity, and that treating ordinary Scarlet Guards as enemies was utterly wrong. Many factories brought them back with gongs and drums. Many factories beat no gongs.

After New Year, one thing followed another. On January 4 the rebels took over Wenhui Daily. On the 5th they took over Liberation Daily too, and the paper ran the “Message to All the People of Shanghai.”

On the 6th there was a mass rally at People's Square. It had a long name, the Rally to Thoroughly Overthrow the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee Headed by Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu. The crowd in the square stretched farther than you could see. The papers later said there were a million.

Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu were dragged onto the stage. A ping-pong table stood on the stage, and they were pushed up onto it to stand so everyone below could see them. Chen Pixian had not recovered from nasopharyngeal cancer. There was gauze taped to his neck and his voice was hoarse. The wind was strong. Someone took their hats off and threw them down off the stage.

Cao Diqiu stood on the ping-pong table looking at his feet the whole time. A little over a month ago, you had waited for him at Culture Square and he did not come. Ten-odd days ago, at Culture Square, he announced that his signature was void. Now he stood on a ping-pong table with his hair blown upright by the wind.

People below threw things up. A rotten cabbage leaf landed by Chen Pixian's feet. Ma Tianshui was on the stage too, half a step behind Chen Pixian, his face gray.

You held a speech that the writing group had written overnight, in very neat handwriting.

History On January 5, Workers' General Headquarters, together with Red Guard and other organizations, nine in all, issued the order “Warmly Welcome the Workers' Scarlet Guards for Defending Mao Zedong Thought Back to Shanghai and Back to the Factories to Take Part in Production.” It had five articles, one of which said “treating ordinary Scarlet Guards as enemies is utterly wrong.” See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 5.

On the 5th they took over Liberation Daily and published the “Message to All the People of Shanghai.” On the 6th the “Rally to Thoroughly Overthrow the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee Headed by Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu” was held at People's Square. Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu were made to stand on a ping-pong table on the outdoor rostrum and were not allowed to wear hats in the cold wind. Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan watched the live television broadcast elsewhere. After the rally the Municipal Party Committee and the city government stopped functioning. See Wikipedia, “January Storm,” and the RFA lecture on the “January Storm” (search summary). Crowd estimates include 100,000 and a million. The million was the propaganda figure of the time.

History Chen Pixian was on sick leave with nasopharyngeal cancer from April to December 1966. See Wikipedia, “Chen Pixian” (search summary).

1062:
The Wave of Economism

From late 1966 into early 1967, temporary workers, contract workers, outsourced workers, and sent-down people who had come back to the city flooded Shanghai's work units with demands to be made permanent, to get back pay, and to return to their original work units. The Municipal Party Committee gave way. Some work units paid out several months' money at once. Long lines formed outside the banks. Hundreds of thousands of tons of goods piled up at the port, and the coal stock at the Yangshupu Power Plant ran out. This wave was later named “economism” and called a new counterattack by the capitalist roaders. History

Wang Hongwen himself took a hard line on it. On January 7, at a headquarters meeting at the No. 31 State Cotton Mill, he called for stopping it at once. That night Workers' General Headquarters issued an “Urgent Order,” and at the liaison station meetings he said the money people had received must be returned, and anyone who did not return it should not join the rebel teams. The same night he proposed setting up a “grasp revolution, promote production” front-line command, with Pan Guoping and Wang Minglong in charge of the railways and docks. His wife Cui Gendi was a temporary nursery worker at the No. 17 Mill nursery. Some said at the time that he was the commander of the temporary workers, but most accounts say he never joined a temporary workers' organization. History See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), chs. 16 and 17.

These demands were rejected wholesale at the time, but some were met later. From 1971, temporary workers who had entered factories before 1966 were made regular workers in batches. Interpretation Li Xun argues that the government's approach only brought people outside the system back into it.

At the headquarters meeting that evening, someone said your political stand was questionable, and someone said you did it for Zhang Chunqiao to see. You answered neither.

On the day at Anting, she had got off the train and asked the people on the tracks why they were stopping it. She had taken three days' leave to go to Nanjing. The train sat at Anting for two days. These days the line at the headquarters door had changed. Fewer came to register as members, and more came for money. History On the evening of January 1, 1967, Cao Diqiu chaired a cadres' meeting on Xiangshan Road and passed on Chen Pixian's words, “ease up on economic issues, don't resist.” It set five points, among them that long-term temporary workers and outsourced workers could become permanent workers and that workers sent down to support agriculture after 1958 could return to their original factories. The Urgent Notice was written by Red Guards, with Zhu Yongjia taking part in the discussion. Geng Jinzhang first signed in the name of Workers' General Headquarters, and later Fan Zuodong signed in his place. On January 10 Mao Zedong wrote the comment “these two pieces are very good.” See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 6, which also reproduces the full text of the notice.

History On January 9, WGHQ and other rebel organizations published the Urgent Notice in Wenhui Daily and Liberation Daily. Its ten articles opposed economism and called it a new counterattack by the bourgeois reactionary line. On January 11 the CCP Central Committee, the State Council, the Central Military Commission and the Central Cultural Revolution Group sent a joint congratulatory telegram calling it “entirely correct.” One account gives 32 signing organizations and another gives 11. Original text not yet checked. See Wikipedia, “January Storm,” and the CCRD database entry (search summary).

History In early 1967 Shanghai saw mass demands for back pay, for making temporary workers permanent, and for sent-down people to return to the city. Some work units handed out money freely, and there were runs on the banks.

History On January 7, at the WGHQ headquarters meeting, Wang Hongwen called for stopping economism at once. That night an “Urgent Order” went out in the name of WGHQ, demanding that all money received be returned. The same night he proposed setting up the front-line command. Cui Gendi was a temporary nursery worker at the No. 17 State Cotton Mill nursery. From 1971 Shanghai made temporary workers who had entered factories before 1966 regular workers in batches. See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), chs. 16 and 17 (paraphrased).

Workers at the Yangshupu Power Plant wept and cheered when they saw the first trainload. Wang Hongwen was not keen on the scramble among the organizations for government offices. Disputed Whether the January power seizure was driven from below by the masses or from above by the Central Cultural Revolution Group is the core question in the scholarly debate. The article “The So-called ‘Shanghai January Revolution’ in the Cultural Revolution,” in Modern China Studies, 2001, no. 2, argues that it was a model manufactured by Mao Zedong.

1114:
⟦0⟧

On the 19th Zhang Chunqiao had you call a meeting of the leaders of the rebel organizations. His idea was that the Municipal Party Committee had collapsed and a new organ of power had to be built, on the principles of the Paris Commune.

⟦1⟧

Three days earlier, at a meeting in Beijing, Chairman Mao had said, if the masses elect new cadres, let them elect. Let them elect factory directors and secretaries. Places that have been taken over can hold elections. When this reached Shanghai, many people copied it into their notebooks.

You had read the words Paris Commune in the Sixteen Points. The Sixteen Points said members of the cultural revolution committees should be chosen through a system of general elections like that of the Paris Commune, and the masses could criticize them at any time, re-elect them and recall them. The first time you read it, you drew a line under those lines.

The meeting went on all day. First the name. Some said call it the New Shanghai Commune. Some said ask Beijing first. Then the quotas. Every organization wanted more seats. The Second Regiment said they had the most people. The Red Revolutionaries students said they had lit the first spark of the January Revolution. Someone pounded the table. Someone slammed the door on the way out and came back after a while.

By evening everyone was tired, and the ashtrays were heaped with cigarette butts. Someone said, how do we settle the quotas, Old Wang, you say something.

1128:
Admitting the Scarlet Guards

On January 21, 1967, WGHQ headquarters met at the No. 31 State Cotton Mill to discuss whether to admit former Scarlet Guards into the rebel teams. The argument ran from six in the evening to six the next morning. Opponents said the conservatives far outnumbered the rebels, and if they were admitted now, they would “swallow up” the rebel teams. Wang Hongwen insisted on admitting them. He said the revolution does not rank people by when they joined, the majority must be united, ordinary Scarlet Guards had been misled, and those who drew a clear line with the past and rose up to rebel should be admitted. In the end his view won. Zhang Chunqiao had also told him several times not to shut the great mass of Scarlet Guards out. But royalists could not serve as the main leaders of rebel teams. This was an unwritten rule. History See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 14.

Li Xun argues that this effectively broke up the rebels' opponents, emotionally and organizationally. In many other provinces and cities, the rebels refused to the end to admit royalists, and the conservatives regrouped under a new banner, like the “Million Heroes” in Wuhan and the “Industrial Army” in Sichuan, and armed fighting went on for years. From then on Shanghai had no opposing organization of that kind. Interpretation

1147:
The January 28 Bombardment

In late January 1967, Fudan's Red Revolutionaries, the Third Headquarters, “Sun Wukong” and other student organizations put up big slogans aimed at Zhang Chunqiao. They had been the first to act in the January power seizure, and they felt the preparations for the new government were shutting students out. On the night of January 29, Zhang Chunqiao called people from Workers' General Headquarters to his residence for a talk, and everything he said hinted that he wanted the workers to step in. Chen Ada spoke up for Zhang. Bao Pao objected on the spot, saying that even if the Red Guards had made mistakes, they should not be met with guns. Wang Hongwen had talked it over with Huang Jinhai beforehand. Both felt they did not know what was behind the bombardment, and they decided to stay out for now and wait and see. That night he said nothing. After the meeting he took people to Fudan to read the big-character posters. Back at the school gate, he found that slogans calling for Zhang Chunqiao's overthrow had been pasted on his own minibus too. History

Beijing settled the matter. On the 29th Mao Zedong did not take his daytime sleep. He waited in the Great Hall of the People for news from Shanghai and had Wang Li draft a telegram. On the morning of the 30th, an extra-urgent telegram from the Central Cultural Revolution Group reached Shanghai. It was the only extra-urgent telegram the CCRG sent to Red Guards in ten years. The Red Revolutionaries stopped that same day, tore down their slogans, released Xu Jingxian and the others they had held, and fell apart after that. History See Li Xun, The Age of Revolutionary Rebellion (《革命造反年代》), ch. 19. Afterward Wang Hongwen cleared out many of the student organizations, saying Red Guards must not be allowed to take control.
